title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review, Operational Tooling, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview:

This document defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for defining and operating SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning guidance, reliability initiative lifecycle, incident review standards, operational tooling conventions, and canonical runbooks. The goal is to provide a single reference that product, platform, and SRE teams can use to write consistent SLOs, respond to incidents, plan capacity for inference workloads, and drive continual reliability improvements.

Scope:
- Applies to all externally-facing inference services (hosted API, dedicated routing, private control plane) and internal control-plane services that affect customer-visible reliability and latency.
- Does not replace product-level feature requirements; it standardizes the reliability contract and operational practices.

Key principles:
- SLOs are customer-facing contracts, expressed in user impact terms (availability, p99 latency, correctness for critical APIs).
- Error budgets are used to balance innovation and reliability: burn triggers remediation or deployment controls.
- Capacity planning must be demand-driven, forecasted, and include emergency runways and automated scaling boundaries.
- Incident reviews (postmortems) must be blameless, timely, and produce measurable action items.
- Runbooks are the canonical, team-owned operational playbooks for common failure modes.

1) SLO and Error Budget Standards

1.1 SLO taxonomy and examples
- Availability (success rate): percentage of requests returning a 2xx response within a functional correctness check window. Example: Hosted Text Generation API SLO = 99.95% success over 30 days.
- Latency (tail and median): p50, p95, p99 measured at the platform ingress after routing and model selection. Example: Chat p99 (short prompts, <=256 tokens) <= 500ms.
- Correctness / Quality guardrails: for deterministic subsystems (embeddings, reranking) track regression metrics tied to evaluation prompt sets (monthly quality SLOs e.g., embedding cosine stability >= 98%).
- Availability by customer tier or region: critical enterprise tenants may have higher SLOs (e.g., 99.99%) with reserved capacity.

1.2 SLO definition template (required)
- Name: short service SLO name
- Owner: service owner (primary oncall team)
- User-facing metric: what the user observes (e.g., request success rate, p99 latency)
- Measurement point: metric name and aggregation (e.g., ingress.request_success_ratio, rolling 30d)
- Target & window: numeric target and rolling window (e.g., 99.95% over 30d)
- Error budget: 1 - target (e.g., 0.05% monthly burn)
- Alerts & burn actions: thresholds for oncall pages and product gating
- Related runbooks and dashboards: link to runbook and dashboard ids

1.3 Alerting and burn policy
- Alert levels:
  - P0 (immediate page): SLO slice breach for core product (e.g., <99.8% over 1h for hosted API) or major traffic loss >5% of baseline within 5 minutes.
  - P1 (notify oncall): sustained error budget burn rate that projects to full burn within 7 days.
  - P2 (ticket): moderate degradation that projects to full burn within 30 days.
- Burn policy steps (automated and human):
  1. Automated mitigation: route to a lower-cost compatible model variant, enable increased batching limits, or use cache fallback where safe.
  2. Immediate oncall investigation when P0 or P1 fires.
  3. If projected burn >75% in 7 days, restrict non-critical deploys to the affected service (deployment freeze) until the budget is restored.
  4. Executive escalation if enterprise tenant SLOs are impacted.

2) Capacity Planning Guidance

2.1 Capacity unit definitions
- Serving capacity is measured in inference capacity units (ICU): the number of concurrent streams of a reference prompt mix that a node type supports at p95 latency under normal operating conditions. ICU normalizes across instance types (e.g., A100-80GB = 20 ICU, H100-80GB = 40 ICU for baseline model family X).
- GPU pool names and tags: use standardized pool names (e.g., pool-hosted-gpu-a100-1, pool-dedicated-h100-ephemeral).

2.2 Planning cadence and runway
- Quarterly forecast: product roadmap + observed growth -> required ICU delta for next quarter (owned by capacity-planning working group).
- Monthly review: verify forecast vs actual utilization and adjust autoscaling targets.
- Emergency runway: maintain a 72-hour provisioning runway (cold-start spin-up including model warm-up) measured in ICU. If reserved pools cannot meet runway, declare capacity shortfall and trigger procurement or cross-region routing.

2.3 Headroom, buffer, and autoscaling settings
- Nominal headroom: maintain 20% buffer on peak expected load for hosted pools to absorb traffic spikes. For enterprise dedicated pools align with contract commitments (minimum 5% buffer or as contractually required).
- Autoscaling: policies must have minimum, target, and maximum ICU. Batching policies must be conservative for low-latency routes.

2.4 Forecasting formula (simple model)
- Required_ICU_next_period = sum_over_routes( baseline_QPS * average_tokens_per_request * tokens_to_throughput_factor ) * safety_multiplier - existing_reserved_ICU
- Document assumptions: prompt mix, token distributions, model family throughput. Archive the calculation and inputs in the capacity planning doc.

3) Reliability Initiatives Lifecycle

3.1 Identification and prioritization
- Sources: incident reviews, SLO burn patterns, customer escalations, performance regressions from CI.
- Scoring: impact (SLO exposure), frequency (how often fire), effort (estimate), and customer severity. Use A*I scoring matrix to prioritize (A=impact, I=frequency).

3.2 Initiative playbook
- Define hypothesis, owner, success metrics (SLO improvement, error budget reduction, cost impact), and timeline (typically 4-12 weeks).
- Run quarterly reliability planning sessions and track initiatives in the reliability board (link to board id).
- Measure with controlled rollouts and guardrails (canary, dark-launch).

4) Incident Review and Postmortem Standards

4.1 Timeline and ownership
- Incident declared -> initial incident report within 2 hours by oncall responder.
- Postmortem draft within 3 business days.
- Final postmortem published and linked to the incident within 10 business days with action items assigned and due dates.

4.2 Postmortem structure (required fields)
- Incident summary (what happened, impact, customer-visible effect)
- Timeline (detailed, minute-level for first hour, then coarse)
- Root cause analysis (technical cause and contributing factors)
- Actions and owners (concrete change, owner, due date)
- Severity classification and SLO impact numeric summary
- Lessons learned and follow-ups (reliability initiatives linked)

4.3 Review process and quality gates
- Triage and validation: the SRE lead validates technical RCA completeness.
- Blameless review: emphasize systemic fixes not individual fault.
- Action item tracking: all actions must be in the task tracker with owners and SLA for completion.

5) Operational Tooling Standards

5.1 Dashboards and metrics
- Canonical dashboards: service-overview (SLOs, error budget projection, top-5 latency histograms), capacity dashboard (ICU utilization, pool headroom), incident timeline dashboard.
- Metric naming conventions: service.<service_name>.<metric> (e.g., service.ingest.p99_latency_ms).

5.2 Alerting and oncall integration
- Single source of truth for alerts: each alert must reference impacted SLO and runbook.
- Pager duty routing: service -> primary oncall -> secondary -> platform SRE escalation.
- Noise reduction: alerts must include suppression windows and frequency thresholds to avoid flapping.

5.3 Automated mitigations and runbook hooks
- Mitigation primitives: routing policy adjust, model fallback, autoscale trigger, cache invalidation, and limited deployment rollback.
- Runbook hooks: automate common first steps (collect logs, run health-check commands) in the alert payload so the oncall can execute with a single click.

5.4 Tooling inventory (minimum required)
| Tool category | Example/tool | Purpose |
|---------------|--------------|---------|
| Monitoring | Prometheus/Grafana | Metrics collection and dashboards |
| Alerting | PagerDuty | Oncall routing and escalation |
| Tracing | Jaeger/Tempo | Distributed tracing for latency RCA |
| Incident Mgmt | Incident board (Jira/Linear) | Track incidents and postmortems |
| Capacity | Capacity planner (internal) | ICU modeling and forecasts |

6) Canonical Runbooks (examples)

6.1 Runbook: High p99 latency on hosted-text-generation
- Symptoms: p99 latency spike > 2x baseline for > 5 minutes, error rate stable.
- Initial checks (first 5 minutes):
  1. Check service-overview dashboard (SLO, error budget projection).
  2. Confirm recent deploys (last 30 minutes) and correlate with rollout.
  3. Check model pool utilization (ICU) and queue depth.
  4. Check GPU node metrics: memory, CPU, NVLink errors.
- Mitigations (order):
  1. Increase serving pool autoscale target by 20% if capacity available.
  2. Route new requests to a compatible, lower-latency model variant (documented compatibility matrix required).
  3. If a rollout is suspected, rollback the last canary.
  4. If queuing is observed, enable short-circuit cache for hot prefixes.
- Escalation: page runtime-owner and infra-oncall if node-level hardware errors seen.
- Follow-up: open postmortem if SLO breached or error budget burned >25% in 24h.

6.2 Runbook: Capacity exhaustion / provisioning failure
- Symptoms: Autoscaler failing to provision nodes, sustained queue growth, or provisioning errors in cloud provider logs.
- Initial checks:
  1. Inspect autoscaler logs and cloud provider quota/limits.
  2. Check recent changes to capacity pool min/max.
  3. Verify model warm-up errors (timeouts during container startup).
- Mitigations:
  1. If quota hit, trigger cross-region failover to alternate pool and inform product owners.
  2. If warm-up delays, deploy a warm pool of placeholders (pre-warmed containers) and gradually attach models.
  3. Apply emergency capacity: bump reserved pool or trigger manual provisioning runbook.
- Follow-up: update capacity forecast and capture improved warm-up procedures.

6.3 Runbook: Elevated error rate (5xx) for API route
- Symptoms: Error rate (5xx) > 0.5% for 10 min or > 0.2% sustained over 1h.
- Initial checks:
  1. Look for correlated deploys or config changes.
  2. Check model health endpoints and container logs for OOMs or exceptions.
  3. Verify upstream dependencies (database, auth, routing service).
- Mitigations:
  1. Fail fast: enable graceful degradation (return cached responses or degrade non-critical features).
  2. Rollback last deploy if correlated.
  3. Throttle low-priority customers using rate-limits to preserve SLO for higher tiers.
- Follow-up: schedule RCA and add regression tests if root cause was change-related.

7) Documentation and Quality Standards for Runbooks and Postmortems
- Ownership: each service must have an up-to-date runbook in Confluence; the service owner is responsible for annual review.
- Format: runbooks use the canonical template with symptoms, initial checks (<=5 items), mitigations (ordered), escalation path, and post-incident follow-up checklist.
- Review cadence: runbooks reviewed quarterly and after any incident.

8) Operational KPIs and Reporting
- Monthly reliability report: SLO attainment, error budget spent per service, top incidents and status of action items, capacity utilization and forecast variance, and active reliability initiatives.
- Executive metrics: rolling 90d SLO attainment for core APIs, number of Sev1 incidents per quarter, average time-to-restore (TTR), and percent of action items completed on time.

Appendices
A. Sample SLO: Hosted Text Generation
- Name: hosted.text_generation.success_rate
- Owner: runtime-team@redwood.example.com
- Metric: ingress.requests.success_ratio (2xx within 10s)
- Target: 99.95% over 30d
- Error budget: 0.05% monthly
- Alerting: page on 1h rolling window < 99.8% or projected full burn in 7d

B. Postmortem checklist (quick)
- Is timeline complete? Are logs and traces attached?
- Is RCA specific and actionable?
- Are actions assigned and dated?
- Has SRE lead validated the doc?

C. Contacts and ownership (examples)
- Runtime service owner: runtime-team@redwood.example.com
- Platform SRE rotations: oncall-platform@redwood.example.com

Document maintenance
- Owner: SRE Documentation Guild (contact: Ari Chen)
- Review cycle: quarterly updates and after-severity incidents.
- Related resources: link to capacity planner, model onboarding docs, and incident board.
summary: Standards and canonical practices for SRE at Redwood: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident reviews, operational tooling, and runbooks.
